Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
The world is a dangerous place
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette:
Arthur, a 78-year-old divorced man and seasoned database administrator, had always prided himself on his meticulous attention to detail. Yet, ever since his life-threatening illness two years ago, he found himself in a world that felt increasingly chaotic and threatening, a stark contrast to the structured environment he had once controlled. The illness had arrived without warning, a sudden diagnosis that had sent him spiraling into a series of treatments, hospital stays, and an overwhelming sense of vulnerability. The sterile smell of antiseptic, so common in hospitals, still lingered in his mind, triggering memories that Arthur wished he could forget.

He recalled the day he first received the diagnosis as if it were happening again, the fluorescent lights buzzing overhead as the doctor explained the severity of his condition. The room felt like it was closing in on him, filled with the sharp scent of alcohol swabs and the clinical chill of fear. As the doctor spoke, Arthur could feel his heart racing, the weight of the words pressing down on him. He had come to believe that his body had betrayed him, that it was a prison filled with threats lurking beneath his skin. This sense of betrayal was compounded by the loneliness of his situation; his ex-wife had long since moved on, and the friends he once relied on seemed distant and preoccupied with their own lives.

In the months following his diagnosis, Arthur became increasingly vigilant. Even within the supposed safety of his own home, he felt an unshakable sense of danger. He would often check the locks on his doors multiple times before bed, a ritual that offered him little solace but became a habit he couldn’t break. The shadows in the corners of his living room felt alive, and every creak of the floorboards turned into an alarm bell in his mind. He was, in his own words, "on guard"—not just for potential intruders, but for the invisible threats he believed lurked in every corner of his existence. 

Arthur's emotions swung like a pendulum; fear and anger seemed to dominate his thoughts. He felt guilt for his perceived weakness, anger at the illness that had altered his life, and a profound sense of horror when he reflected on the fragility of life. Each day was a struggle against a tide of negative feelings that left him drained. He often sat in his living room, staring at the walls that felt like they were closing in on him, grappling with the notion that the world outside was a dangerous place where he could no longer trust anyone, not even himself. 

The memories of his hospitalization haunted him in ways he never anticipated. Arthur often found himself swept away in vivid recollections of the sterile hospital room, the beeping machines, and the nurses who came and went with their clinical detachment. The scent of antiseptic would invade his thoughts unexpectedly, transporting him back to those harrowing days when he felt the life slipping away from him. It was as if he were reliving the event in real-time, his heart racing and palms sweating as he fought to escape the suffocating grip of those memories. Ordinary moments felt trivial and distant in comparison; his recollections of the illness were more tangible, more real. 

This relentless cycle of hypervigilance and negative emotions took a toll on Arthur's everyday life. His work, once a source of pride and accomplishment, became a battleground of anxiety. He found himself avoiding social interactions with colleagues, fearing that even casual conversations would draw him back into the depths of his trauma. Meetings felt overwhelming, filled with a sense of impending doom that left him retreating to his desk, where he could hide behind the glow of his computer screen. The isolation he created only deepened his mistrust of the world, and he was convinced that people could not understand the turmoil raging within him.

It was only when Arthur found himself in tears one evening, overwhelmed by the weight of his emotions, that he realized he could no longer navigate this path alone. The fear that had once been a quiet whisper became a deafening roar, urging him to seek help. He hoped for relief, for the possibility of reclaiming a sense of safety and trust in a world that had felt so hostile for far too long. What frightened him most was the thought that he might forever be trapped in this cycle of fear and isolation, but a faint glimmer of hope nudged him toward the idea that perhaps healing was possible, if only he could find the right support.
